newsitem.title: FRANCE: Brittan hopes for US-EU product recognition deal.
newsitem.headline: Brittan hopes for US-EU product recognition deal.

text.p: European Foreign Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Monday he still hoped to strike a deal with the United States so that pharmaceutical and other products certified in the European Union would not need double-checking in the United States and vice-versa.

A U.S. official said on Sunday the most recent negotiations had failed to produce a deal but Brittan said that he would meet U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on the sidelines of an OECD meeting here on Tuesday to try to move ahead.
"We're working on it. We're not at an agreement yet but we hope to get there," Brittan, who represents the European Union in international free trade talks, told reporters.

The talks covered so-called mutual recognition agreements that would allow agencies in the United States to perform procedures like testing, inspection and certification to EU requirements, and vice versa, and eliminate the need for checks to be carried out twice.

The areas covered in the negotiations, in which the latest round was held last week in Washington, include pharmaceuticals, medical devices, telecommunications, information technology and sports craft.

An EU official said the main trouble spots were in the domain of pharmaceutical products and medical devices but that there had been a lot of progress in telecommunications and on recreational craft such as speedboats.

One of the main problems from the EU perspective was that the main U.S. certifying agency concerned, the Food and Drug Administration, was insisting it be able to carry out individual checks on EU agencies, even when those agencies had already been cleared as of equivalent standard.
It also wanted the right to renege on the agreement in any given sector and was not keen to accept the pace which Brittan was seeking on the number of products that would be covered.

One U.S. official close to last week's talks said that from the U.S. point of view the main sticking points were the EU demands on testing and certification of pharmaceuticals products and medical equipment, which the United States believed would lower U.S. consumer standards.
